 1                 II.   PURPOSE AND SUMMARY OF TESTIMONY

 2   Q.   What is the purpose of your testimony in this phase of the case?

 3   A.   I am providing testimony in support of the Comprehensive Stipulation

 4        (“Stipulation”), particularly Sections 1.11, 1.13, 1.14, 1.15, 1.16, 1.18, 1.19, and

 5        1.20. Specifically, my testimony will:

 6             •    support the rates designed to recover the base rate revenue requirement
 7                  assigned to each customer class as reflected in the Proof of Revenue and
 8                  stipulated revenue allocation in Exhibit A to the Stipulation;

 9             •    discuss and support the rate design and tariff provisions in Section 1.13
10                  of the Stipulation, including modification of the Large General Service
11                  Transmission (“LGS-T”) demand ratchet from 60% to 70%, continuation
12                  of the power factor credit for the LGS-T class, and approval of other rate
13                  design aspects of SPS’s proposed tariffs (except as addressed in Section
14                  1.16);

15             •    discuss and support the Renewable*Connect Tariff modifications in
16                  Section 1.14 of the Stipulation, including the structure of the Unbundled
17                  Production Credit;

18             •    discuss and support approval of the Time-of-Use Fuel Pilot in Section
19                  1.15 of the Stipulation;

20             •    discuss and support the Standby Rate 85 provisions in Section 1.16 of the
21                  Stipulation, including the standby generation demand charge at 10% of
22                  the applicable LGS-T generation demand rate and the correction to
23                  maintain consistency with the existing Option 1 rate structure and Rate
24                  34 revenue neutrality;

25             •    discuss and support the Western Area Power Administration (“WAPA”)

 1        III.   CUSTOMER CLASS BASE RATE REVENUE DISTRIBUTION

 2   Q.    Please summarize the customer class base revenue distribution that is

 3         contained in Section 1.11 of the Stipulation.

 4   A.    Section 1.11 of the Stipulation discusses the stipulated base revenue distribution

 5         among the New Mexico retail customer classes. The specific revenue responsibility

 6         of each customer class is presented on page 1 of Exhibit A to the Stipulation. This

 7         distribution of the base rate revenue increase among customer classes reflects the

 8         consensus agreement that resulted from negotiations among the Signatories.

 9   Q.    Does Exhibit A to the Stipulation provide a complete picture of how the settled

10         revenue allocation was developed?

11   A.    Exhibit A presents the final settled base rate revenue distribution by customer class

12         and the resulting proof of revenue. However, it does not show the underlying

13         comparison between a strict Class Cost of Service Study (“CCOSS”) based

14         allocation of the $90 million base rate increase and the actual settled allocation. To

15         provide greater transparency into the gradualism adjustments embedded in the

16         Stipulation, I am also sponsoring Attachment AGT-STIP-1.

 1   Q.   What additional information does Attachment AGT-STIP-1 provide?

 2   A.   Attachment AGT-STIP-1 presents the following:

 3             •    The base rate revenue increase that would result from applying the
 4                  CCOSS directly to the stipulated $90 million base rate increase, using the
 5                  class demand and energy billing determinants from the Future Test Year;

 6             •    The actual settled base rate revenue increase allocated to each customer
 7                  class under the Stipulation;

 8             •    The difference between the CCOSS outcome and the settled allocation,
 9                  which illustrates the amount of gradualism support being provided or
10                  received by each class, and;

11             •    The resulting impact on each class’s total revenue requirement after
12                  reflecting the corresponding changes in Fuel and Purchase Power Cost
13                  Adjustment Clause and other rider revenues.

14             This attachment shows that, relative to a pure CCOSS allocation, residential

15        and small commercial classes receive meaningful reductions in their base rate

16        increase responsibility, while certain industrial classes provide gradualism support

17        through higher allocations. It helps demonstrate that the stipulated revenue

18        allocation reflects a reasonable compromise that balances cost causation principles

19        with the mitigation of customer bill impacts.

 3   Q.   Do you believe the customer class base rate revenue distribution is reasonable?

 4   A.   Yes. The Signatories expressed differing views in their testimony concerning

 5        adjustments to SPS’s costs and presented differing positions on the allocation of

 6        the costs of the Hale and Sagamore wind projects and various other cost

 7        components. The parties also expressed differing opinions in their testimony

 8        concerning gradualism methodologies. The customer class base rate revenue

 9        distribution that is provided in Section 1.11 to the Stipulation reflects a negotiated

10        resolution of these various differences among all of the Signatories and is a

11        reasonable compromise.

12   Q.   Does Section 1.11 of the Stipulation violate any important regulatory principle

13        or practice?

14   A.   No. Section 1.11 of the Stipulation is consistent with existing regulatory principles

15        and practices and does not require any exception from any Commission rule or

16        practice. In addition, as discussed by SPS witness Zoë E. Lees, the Commission has

17        stated that it favors settlements to avoid costly and protracted litigation and that a

 1             IV.    STIPULATION RATE DESIGN AND TARIFFS

 2   Q.   Please summarize the Stipulation rate design.

 3   A.   The Stipulation rate design is presented in Sections 1.11 and 1.13 to the Stipulation,

 4        and the proposed rates are included in the Proof of Revenue that is provided at

 5        pages 2 through 6 of Exhibit A to the Stipulation. The Proof of Revenue

 6        demonstrates the rates are designed to recover the base rate revenue requirement

 7        assigned to each customer class and the total New Mexico base rate revenue

 8        requirement from all customer classes. The Signatories reviewed the Proof of

 9        Revenue and revised tariffs prior to the filing of the Stipulation, and agreed that the

10        rates are consistent with the terms of the Stipulation.

11   Q.   Do the proposed charges result in reasonable ranges of impacts for each rate?

12   A.   Yes. Attachment AGT-STIP-2 to this testimony provides a comparison of each

13        proposed rate to the present rates. In addition, Attachment AGT-STIP-3 to this

14        testimony contains a bill impact comparison that shows the range of impacts for

15        each of the rates is reasonable.

 1   Q.   Does the Stipulation address any other rate design issues?

 2   A.   Yes. As set forth in Section 1.13 of the Stipulation, SPS will modify the current

 3        LGS-T 60% ratchet demand to a 70% ratchet demand. SPS will continue to provide

 4        its power factor credit for the LGS-T class.

 5               The move from the current 60% ratchet to 70% represents a reasonable

 6        compromise. Through my direct testimony, SPS proposed increasing the LGS-T

 7        ratchet to 85% to better align with cost causation, reduce intra-class subsidization,

 8        stabilize revenues, and allow for lower demand rates while protecting against

 9        under-recovery from variable loads. The stipulated 70% level moves meaningfully

10        in the direction of SPS’s proposal—improving cost recovery alignment and

11        equity—while moderating the impact on customers relative to the full 85% request.

12               SPS will also continue the existing power factor credit for the LGS-T class,

13        preserving the current structure that provides an incentive for customers to maintain

14        efficient power factor performance above 0.95. The Signatories reached the

15        stipulated rate design through compromise of the issues raised in this case without

16        specifically accepting or rejecting, for purposes of this Stipulation, any ratemaking

17        issue or principle.

 1                    V.    RENEWABLE*CONNECT TARIFF

 2   Q.   Please describe the changes to the Renewable*Connect Tariff rate in Section

 3        1.14 of the Stipulation.

 4   A.   Section 1.14 of the Stipulation provides the Renewable*Connect Unbundled

 5        Production Credit will be equivalent to the demand charge less the Unbundled

 6        Transmission Demand Charges. To achieve this, SPS subtracts the Unbundled

 7        Transmission Demand Charge, which is calculated as part of the Standby service

 8        rates, from the standard LGS-T 115 kV winter and summer demand charges.

 9   Q.   Why is this treatment reasonable?

10   A.   The Unbundled Production Credit structure properly unbundles the production

11        component and aligns the credit calculation with the underlying Standby Rate 85

12        transmission demand charges. This promotes transparency and consistency for the

13        Renewable*Connect program, while providing appropriate credits to participating

14        customers. The Signatories support this as fair and reasonable.

 1                       VI.    TIME-OF-USE FUEL PILOT

 2   Q.   What does the Stipulation provide regarding the Time-of-Use Fuel Pilot?

 3   A.   Section 1.15 of the Stipulation provides that the Signatories agree that SPS’s

 4        proposed time-of-use (“TOU”) fuel pilot is reasonable and should be approved.

 5   Q.   Why should the TOU Fuel Pilot be approved?

 6   A.   The TOU fuel pilot provides participating customers with the opportunity to

 7        manage their fuel cost exposure through time-differentiated pricing, which can

 8        encourage more efficient use of the system during off-peak periods and provide

 9        price signals that better reflect the time-varying nature of fuel and purchased power

10        costs. Approval of the pilot is consistent with the public interest in exploring

11        innovative rate designs that can benefit customers and improve system utilization.

12        No party opposes approval of the pilot under the Stipulation.

 1                           VII.     STANDBY RATE 85

 2   Q.   Please summarize the Standby Rate 85 provisions in Section 1.16 of the

 3        Stipulation.

 4   A.   The standby generation demand charge will continue to be designed equal to 10%

5         of the applicable LGS-T generation demand rate. SPS will correct the proposed

6         Rate 85 rate design to maintain consistency with the existing Option 1 rate

7         structure, under which total revenues from standby demand and backup energy

8         charges would be the same for a customer with no onsite solar production as they

9         would be under Rate 34.

10   Q.   Why are these provisions reasonable and in the public interest?

11   A.   Maintaining the standby generation demand charge at 10% of the LGS-T generation

12        demand rate continues the existing policy for interruptible/standby service. The

13        correction to the proposed Rate 85 rate design ensures revenue neutrality and

14        consistency with Rate 34 for customers without onsite generation, preventing

15        unintended shifts in cost recovery or customer impacts. This correction aligns the

16        tariff with rate design principles. The Signatories support these provisions as a

17        reasonable resolution of the standby tariff issues.

1                            VIII.    WAPA CREDITS

2    Q.   What does Section 1.18 of the Stipulation provide regarding WAPA Credits?

3    A.   Section 1.18 provides that the credits included in the SLCA Rider No. 27 shall be

4         set equal to the production capacity costs included in the LGS-T 115 kV demand

5         and energy charges. Similar to the Renewable*Connect Unbundled Production

6         Credit, the production capacity costs included in the LGS-T 115 kV are calculated

7         by subtracting the Unbundled Transmission Demand Charge, which is calculated

 8        as part of the Standby service rates, from the standard LGS-T 115 kV winter and

 9        summer demand charges.

10   Q.   Why is this alignment reasonable?

11   A.   Setting the SLCA Rider credits equal to the production capacity costs embedded in

12        the LGS-T 115 kV rates ensures that the credits provided to qualifying customers

13        accurately reflect the underlying cost of service for production capacity. This

14        treatment is consistent with cost causation principles and provides appropriate and

15        transparent crediting for customers served under the SLCA Rider. It represents a

16        reasonable and straightforward resolution of the WAPA credit issue in this

17        proceeding.

 1        IX.   PUBLIC ELECTRIC VEHICLE DIRECT CURRENT FAST
 2                            CHARGING RATE

 3   Q.    What commitments does SPS make in Section 1.19 of the Stipulation regarding

4          public electric vehicle (“EV”) DCFC rates?

5    A.    SPS agrees to collaborate with Walmart and other interested stakeholders regarding

6          the development of a new electric vehicle rate specifically designed for public-

7          facing DCFC facilities. SPS shall initiate a stakeholder process within 60 days

8          following the Commission’s final order in this proceeding and report on that

9          process in its next Transportation Electrification Plan (“TEP”) filing. Based on

10         those workshops, SPS shall file a proposed DCFC-specific rate, tariff, or rate design

11         with the Commission.

12   Q.    Why is this collaborative approach reasonable?

13   A.    Public DCFC facilities have unique load characteristics—high demand, low load

14         factor, and usage patterns that may not align well with existing commercial or

15         industrial rate designs. A dedicated DCFC rate can better reflect cost causation,

16         avoid inappropriate cost shifts, and support the growth of public EV charging

17         infrastructure consistent with state and federal policy goals. The collaborative

18         stakeholder process ensures that the rate design benefits from input by Walmart (a

 1              X.     DATA CENTERS AND LARGE LOAD TARIFFS

 2   Q.   What does Section 1.20 of the Stipulation require regarding Data Centers and

 3        Large Load Tariffs?

 4   A.   SPS shall develop and file for Commission approval a new Large Load customer

 5        class and tariff within six months following the Commission’s final order in this

 6        proceeding and include the Large Load customer class in its cost-of-service study

 7        in its next base rate case, to the extent that such a tariff is approved by the

 8        Commission prior to the filing of that next base rate case. The proposed class and

 9        tariff shall be designed to ensure that all costs attributable to serving Large Load

10        customers are assigned to that class and do not shift costs or risks to any other

11        customer class. SPS will gather intervenor input on the Large Load tariff before

12        filing it.

13   Q.   Why is the development of a dedicated Large Load tariff important and

14        reasonable?

15   A.   Large Load customers, such as data centers and other hyperscale operations, may

16        present distinct load profiles, growth patterns, and infrastructure requirements that

17        differ significantly from traditional commercial and industrial customers. A

18        dedicated tariff allows for precise assignment of costs—including any incremental

 2        those costs. This protects other customer classes from potential cost shifts or risks

 3        associated with serving these loads. The six-month timeline ensures timely

 4        development while allowing adequate time for stakeholder input, which will

 5        improve the quality and acceptance of the proposal. Including the cost allocation

 6        proposal in the next cost-of-service study, if approved in time, promotes

 7        transparency and consistency in future rate proceedings. This approach is consistent

 8        with emerging practices in other jurisdictions facing similar large load growth and

 9        represents a proactive, customer-protective step that is in the public interest.
